country.name: Austria
country.tagline: Grüner Veltliner on Danube terraces, Blaufränkisch in Pannonian heat, and a wine country reborn from scandal into one of Europe's most rigorous.

stats.note: OIV State of the World Wine Sector in 2025 (2.5 mhl, 17th in the OIV table); Statistik Austria counted 2.56 mhl for 2025, the biggest crop since 2018. Vineyard area 44,210 ha per Austrian Wine and Advantage Austria.

country.overview:
Austria makes wine only in its east, where the Alps drop to the Danube and the Pannonian plain, and almost all of its 44,210 hectares lie in four federal states: Niederösterreich (Lower Austria), Burgenland, Steiermark (Styria) and Wien (Vienna). That small area holds a surprising range of climates. Cool air drains off the forested Waldviertel into the Danube valley at night; hot, dry continental summers bake the plains around Lake Neusiedl; and warm, wet Mediterranean influence reaches the steep green hills of southern Styria on the Slovenian border. So Austria does crisp whites, serious reds and some of the world's great sweet wines with equal conviction.

Grüner Veltliner is the national grape, on about a third of the vineyard (32.3 percent). It can be a light, peppery tavern wine for a summer evening or a dense single-vineyard white from the Wachau, Kamptal or Kremstal that stands beside white Burgundy and ages for twenty years. Riesling covers far fewer hectares but gives some of the country's most profound wines on the stony Danube terraces. Among reds, Zweigelt (13.4 percent, a 1922 Klosterneuburg crossing) is the everyday favourite, while Blaufränkisch (5.8 percent) is Austria's most expressive red, a grape that shows its soil the way Pinot Noir does, at its best in Mittelburgenland, on the Leithaberg and at Eisenberg. Welschriesling, Sankt Laurent, Pinot Noir, the Thermenregion's Zierfandler and Rotgipfler, Styria's Sauvignon Blanc and Gelber Muskateller, and Vienna's Gemischter Satz field blends complete the picture.

The defining event of modern Austrian wine was a disaster. In 1985 German laboratories found diethylene glycol in Austrian wines on German supermarket shelves; a small group of brokers had been adding it to fake the richness of expensive late-harvest wines. Germany issued a health warning, Japan banned Austrian wine outright, and exports collapsed from about 45 million litres a year to 4.4 million in 1986. Parliament passed what was then Europe's strictest wine law within weeks, a national marketing board was set up, and a generation of growers turned from cheap sweet wine to dry, terroir-driven quality. Export volumes only regained their pre-scandal level around 2001, but the wines that came back were far better than those that left.

Since 2002 Austria has built a French-style appellation system, the DAC (Districtus Austriae Controllatus), region by region. The Weinviertel was first; with the Thermenregion in 2023, all of the country's specific wine-growing areas were covered by 18 DACs, each with rules about grapes and style that tell the drinker what the place stands for. Most use a Burgundy-like pyramid of regional wine (Gebietswein), village wine (Ortswein) and single-vineyard wine (Riedenwein). Private groups classified the best sites first (Vinea Wachau, the ÖTW in the Danube regions, Styria's STK), and a 2023 ordinance created the legal basis for official Erste Lage and Große Lage vineyards, region by region, from 2025 onward.

Austria is also a leader in green farming: 10,432 hectares, a quarter of the vineyard, are certified organic, one of the highest shares of any wine country, and biodynamics has deep roots from Nikolaihof in the Wachau to the Pannobile growers of Gols. The Heuriger, the tavern where growers sell their own young wine under a bunch of pine twigs, keeps wine part of daily life, above all in Vienna, the only world capital with a serious wine industry inside its city limits. The 2025 harvest was generous (2.56 million hectolitres, 37 percent more than the frost- and hail-hit 2024) and, as in most recent vintages, the quality was high. Exports reached 60.6 million litres worth 218.9 million euros.

history.title: Grape seeds at Zagersdorf
history.text: Seeds of cultivated grapes from a Hallstatt-era burial mound at Zagersdorf in Burgenland are among the oldest evidence of viticulture in central Europe. Celtic bronze wine flagons of the fifth century BC turned up at the Dürrnberg near Hallein.

history.title: Romans on the Danube
history.text: The Romans held the Danube frontier from Carnuntum and Favianis (Mautern). Emperor Probus (276 to 282) is credited with lifting limits on vine planting north of the Alps, and viticulture spread through Noricum and Pannonia.

history.title: Klosterneuburg founded
history.text: Margrave Leopold III founded the Augustinian abbey of Klosterneuburg, still Austria's largest private wine estate after about 900 years. Bavarian and Austrian abbeys (Tegernsee, Niederaltaich, Göttweig, Melk, Zwettl) built the Wachau and Kamptal terraces.

history.title: The first named vineyard
history.text: The Kremser Sandgrube (1208) and the Steiner Pfaffenberg (1230) are the oldest recorded vineyard names in Austria, proof that the single site has been a unit of value here for eight centuries.

history.title: The Ungeld
history.text: Duke Rudolf IV introduced the Ungeld, the first tax on wine sold in taverns, a sign of how central wine was to the medieval economy of Vienna and Lower Austria.

history.title: Rust buys its freedom with wine
history.text: The lakeside town of Rust paid Emperor Leopold I a large sum in gold and a quantity of its prized Ausbruch sweet wine to become a royal free town, a status it still holds as Austria's smallest statutory city.

history.title: Joseph II's Heuriger decree
history.text: Emperor Joseph II allowed all residents to sell wine and juice they had made themselves, founding the Heuriger and Buschenschank tavern tradition.

history.title: Klosterneuburg school and phylloxera
history.text: The wine school at Klosterneuburg (1860), one of the oldest in the world, gave Austria the KMW must-weight scale. Phylloxera was found in Austria in 1872; replanting favoured Grüner Veltliner.

history.title: Zweigelt is crossed
history.text: Friedrich Zweigelt crossed Sankt Laurent with Blaufränkisch at Klosterneuburg. The grape, first called Rotburger, became Austria's most planted red. Zweigelt's Nazi party record has since led some growers to call for the old name again.

history.title: Lenz Moser's high culture
history.text: Lenz Moser III at Rohrendorf promoted wide-spaced, high-trained vines (Hochkultur), which cut labour costs and were adopted across Austria and abroad.

history.title: The glycol scandal
history.text: Diethylene glycol was found in Austrian wines in German supermarkets from late June 1985. A German health warning followed on 9 July and Japan banned Austrian wine. A strict new wine law passed on 29 August 1985. Exports fell to a tenth and took about 15 years to recover.

history.title: Vinea Wachau and Smaragd
history.text: Wachau growers founded Vinea Wachau in 1983 and adopted the Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd categories for unchaptalised dry wines; Smaragd was first used in 1986.

history.title: Two wine landscapes on the UNESCO list
history.text: The Wachau Cultural Landscape was inscribed in 2000 and the Fertő/Neusiedlersee Cultural Landscape in 2001.

history.title: The DAC system
history.text: Weinviertel DAC (from the 2002 vintage) began the system; Thermenregion DAC (2023 vintage) completed it at 18 DACs. A 2023 ordinance created the legal basis for official Erste and Große Lagen.

country.classification:
Austrian labels mix three layers, and the most useful is origin.

DAC. Each of the 18 DACs fixes the grapes and style that may use the regional name; anything else from the same place is sold under the broader federal-state origin (Niederösterreich, Burgenland, Steiermark, Wien). A Kamptal DAC is therefore always Grüner Veltliner or Riesling, a Mittelburgenland DAC always Blaufränkisch, a Weststeiermark DAC usually Schilcher. Most DACs now use three tiers: Gebietswein (regional), Ortswein (village) and Riedenwein (single vineyard, labelled 'Ried' plus the site name), with stricter yields, later release dates and often hand harvesting higher up. A 2023 collective ordinance lets each region classify Rieden as Erste Lage and, at least five years later, Große Lage, with criteria including history, homogeneity of soil and climate, market value and critical reputation; the terms may appear only on DAC wines.

Quality levels. Qualitätswein (including the light, unchaptalised Kabinett) and Prädikatswein, graded by must weight in degrees KMW (Klosterneuburger Mostwaage): Spätlese (19), Auslese (21), Eiswein, Strohwein or Schilfwein (straw- or reed-dried grapes) and Beerenauslese (25), Ausbruch (27) and Trockenbeerenauslese (30).

Private classifications. In the Wachau, Vinea Wachau's Steinfeder (up to 11.5 percent alcohol), Federspiel (11.5 to 12.5) and Smaragd (above 12.5) describe ripeness for unchaptalised dry wines. The ÖTW (Österreichische Traditionsweingüter, founded 1991, 78 members by 2023) has used 'ÖTW Erste Lage' since the 2009 vintage for top Danube-region sites, and Styria's STK and Burgenland groups such as Pannobile and Renommierte Weingüter Burgenland apply their own rules.
country.climate_soils:
Austria's vineyards meet three climatic forces. The Pannonian plain to the east pushes hot, dry summers and cold winters into Burgenland, the Weinviertel and the Thermenregion. Along the Danube, cool northern air from the Waldviertel plateau drops into the valleys at night, preserving acidity and aroma in Wachau, Kremstal and Kamptal wines. In Styria, Mediterranean influence brings more rain and warmth, so grapes grow on steep, well-drained slopes to avoid rot.

Soils are just as varied. The Danube terraces sit on the crystalline rocks of the Bohemian Massif (gneiss, amphibolite, mica schist, granulite), often covered by loess; the Kamptal's Heiligenstein is Permian desert sandstone. The Weinviertel is mostly loess, with limestone and the Waschberg klippen. Lake Neusiedl's eastern shore is sand, gravel and saline soils; the Leithagebirge is Leitha limestone and schist; Mittelburgenland has heavy, deep clays; Eisenberg has greenschist and iron-rich loam. Southern Styria's opok (calcareous marl and sandstone) and schist contrast with the basalt and tuff of the Vulkanland.

Lake Neusiedl, a steppe lake under two metres deep and 315 square kilometres in area, warms the region and its autumn mists favour noble rot, making Burgenland one of the most reliable botrytis areas in the world.

grapes.name: Grüner Veltliner
grapes.note: About 32 percent of the vineyard. Peppery and fresh in the Weinviertel, deep and mineral on the Danube. Its parents are Traminer and an ancient vine found at St. Georgen in the Leithagebirge.

grapes.name: Zweigelt
grapes.note: About 13 percent; juicy, cherry-fruited red, the backbone of Neusiedlersee DAC and much Carnuntum and Weinviertel red.

grapes.name: Welschriesling
grapes.note: About 6 percent; crisp everyday white in Styria and Burgenland and a great botrytis grape around Lake Neusiedl. Unrelated to Riesling.

grapes.name: Blaufränkisch
grapes.note: About 6 percent; Austria's noblest red, peppery, dark-fruited and site-sensitive, dominant in Mittelburgenland, Eisenberg, Leithaberg and Rosalia.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.note: A small share of the vineyard but the summit of Wachau, Kremstal and Kamptal quality.

grapes.name: Zierfandler and Rotgipfler
grapes.note: Thermenregion specialities around Gumpoldskirchen, often blended as Spätrot-Rotgipfler.

grapes.name: Sankt Laurent and Pinot Noir
grapes.note: Thermenregion and northern Burgenland reds of growing finesse.

grapes.name: Blauer Wildbacher
grapes.note: The source of Schilcher, West Styria's searingly fresh rosé.

grapes.name: Roter Veltliner, Neuburger, Weißburgunder, Chardonnay (Morillon)
grapes.note: Supporting whites; Roter Veltliner is a Wagram speciality, Morillon is the Styrian name for Chardonnay.

regions.name: Niederösterreich
regions.tagline: The Danube's terraces and the Weinviertel's loess: Austria's white-wine heartland.
regions.summary:
Lower Austria holds 26,732 hectares, about 60 percent of the country's vineyard, and produced 1.7 million hectolitres in 2025. It contains eight specific wine areas, each now a DAC. Along the Danube west of Vienna lie the famous three: the Wachau, Kremstal and Kamptal, plus the smaller Traisental and the Wagram's loess terraces. North of the river, the vast Weinviertel ('wine quarter') stretches to the Czech border and alone produced almost a million hectolitres in 2025. South-east of Vienna lie Carnuntum, with its Roman ruins and Zweigelt, and the Thermenregion, the spa country of Baden bei Wien with its rare white grapes and Pinot.

Grüner Veltliner rules here, from the 'Pfefferl' of the Weinviertel to the Smaragd of the Wachau, with Riesling in the stony Danube sites. The region's wine culture is visible everywhere in its Kellergassen, lanes of small press houses and cellars dug into loess at the edge of villages.
regions.history: Roman forts on the Danube (Favianis, Carnuntum), then monasteries (Klosterneuburg, Göttweig, Melk, Zwettl, Herzogenburg) and Bavarian abbeys shaped the vineyards. Krems and Stein were medieval wine-trading towns. The twentieth century brought Lenz Moser's high-trained vines at Rohrendorf, then the post-1985 quality revolution led by growers like Josef Jamek, F.X. Pichler, Emmerich Knoll and Willi Bründlmayer.
regions.terroir: Crystalline rocks of the Bohemian Massif on the Danube terraces, loess everywhere else, limestone at Falkenstein and in the Thermenregion; a meeting of cool Waldviertel air and warm Pannonian influence.
regions.grapes: Grüner Veltliner, Riesling, Zweigelt, Welschriesling, Weißburgunder, Blauer Portugieser, Roter Veltliner, Zierfandler, Rotgipfler, Sankt Laurent, Pinot Noir.
regions.styles: Dry whites dominate; reds in Carnuntum, the Thermenregion and the Weinviertel; Sekt (much Austrian Sekt g.U. comes from here).
regions.classification: Eight DACs: Wachau, Kremstal, Kamptal, Traisental, Wagram, Weinviertel, Carnuntum, Thermenregion. Wines outside DAC rules are labelled Niederösterreich. ÖTW Erste Lagen cover the Danube regions.

regions.name: Burgenland
regions.tagline: Pannonian heat, a steppe lake and Austria's greatest reds and sweet wines.
regions.summary:
Burgenland runs down Austria's eastern border with Hungary and has 11,538 hectares of vines. It became Austrian only in 1921, and its culture still faces east. Around Lake Neusiedl the Pannonian climate is the warmest and driest in the country, and the lake's autumn mists make it one of the most reliable places on earth for noble rot. The region is Austria's red-wine heartland: Zweigelt around the lake, Blaufränkisch in Mittelburgenland, on the Leithaberg and at Eisenberg, plus Sankt Laurent and Pinot Noir.

Its five wine areas are Neusiedlersee (the eastern shore and Seewinkel), Leithaberg (the western shore and the Leitha hills), Rosalia, Mittelburgenland and Eisenberg in the south, along with the sweet-wine DAC of Ruster Ausbruch. In 2025 Burgenland produced 582,900 hectolitres, slightly more than half of it red.
regions.history: Hallstatt-era grape seeds at Zagersdorf, Roman villas, and the Hungarian nobility (the Esterházy family still owns large estates) shaped the region. Rust's Ausbruch was among Europe's most prized sweet wines in the seventeenth century. Burgenland was the epicentre of the 1985 glycol scandal and then of the recovery, through growers such as Alois Kracher, Ernst Triebaumer, Hans Igler, Josef Umathum and the Gols group Pannobile.
regions.terroir: Flat sand, gravel, black earth and salty Seewinkel soils east of the lake; Leitha limestone and mica schist on the Leithagebirge; heavy clay in Mittelburgenland; greenschist and iron-rich loam at Eisenberg.
regions.grapes: Zweigelt, Blaufränkisch, Welschriesling, Grüner Veltliner, Sankt Laurent, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Weißburgunder, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Furmint (revived at Rust).
regions.styles: Dry reds and red blends, dry whites, rosé, and noble sweet wines (Ausbruch, BA, TBA, Eiswein, Schilfwein).
regions.classification: DACs: Neusiedlersee, Leithaberg, Rosalia, Mittelburgenland, Eisenberg, Ruster Ausbruch. Other wines are labelled Burgenland.

regions.name: Steiermark
regions.tagline: Steep green hills on the Slovenian border, built for Sauvignon Blanc.
regions.summary:
Styria has 5,109 hectares of vines on some of the steepest slopes in Austria, a landscape of forested hills, wooden rattles (Klapotetz) to scare off birds and Buschenschank taverns. The climate is warmer and wetter than the Danube, with Mediterranean influence from the south and strong day-night swings, and the wines are aromatic, crisp and dry. Sauvignon Blanc is the star, alongside Gelber Muskateller, Morillon (Chardonnay), Weißburgunder and Welschriesling. Three DACs divide the region: Südsteiermark, Vulkanland Steiermark and Weststeiermark, home of Schilcher rosé.

A generation of growers (Tement, Polz, Gross, Sattlerhof, Lackner-Tinnacher, Wohlmuth) built an international reputation for Styrian Sauvignon from the 1990s on, while a group of natural-wine pioneers (Sepp and Maria Muster, Ewald Tscheppe of Werlitsch, Andreas Tscheppe, Franz Strohmeier) made the region a reference for skin-contact and biodynamic wines.
regions.history: The Styrian vineyard grew under the Habsburgs and the Archduke Johann (1782 to 1859), who promoted modern viticulture. Much of southern Styria lost its vineyards to the new border with Yugoslavia in 1919, and some estates still own vines on the Slovenian side.
regions.terroir: Opok (calcareous marl and sandstone), sand, gravel and schist in the south; basalt and volcanic tuff in the south-east; gneiss and schist in the west. High rainfall is offset by steep, well-drained slopes.
regions.grapes: Welschriesling, Sauvignon Blanc, Weißburgunder, Morillon, Gelber Muskateller, Grauburgunder, Traminer, Blauer Wildbacher, Zweigelt.
regions.styles: Dry aromatic whites, Schilcher rosé and Schilcher sparkling, skin-contact and natural wines.
regions.classification: Three DACs from the 2018 vintage, each with Gebietswein, Ortswein and Riedenwein tiers; the STK producers' group classifies its own Große and Erste STK Rieden.

regions.name: Wien
regions.tagline: A world capital with 588 hectares of vines and a tavern on every hill.
regions.summary:
Vienna has 588 hectares of vineyards inside the city limits, on the slopes of the Kahlenberg, Nussberg and Bisamberg north of the Danube and at Mauer in the south. The city's signature is the Wiener Gemischter Satz, a white field blend of several varieties grown, picked and fermented together, which became a DAC in 2013. The Heurigen of Grinzing, Sievering, Nussdorf, Heiligenstadt, Stammersdorf and Neustift serve young wine with cold cuts under the 'ausg'steckt' pine branch, a tradition founded by Joseph II's decree of 17 August 1784.

Fritz Wieninger, Rainer Christ, Richard Zahel and the Mayer am Pfarrplatz estate (in the house where Beethoven lived in 1817) led a revival that turned Vienna from tourist wine into a serious appellation. In 2025 the city produced 30,200 hectolitres.
regions.history: Vines have grown in Vienna since Roman Vindobona. Medieval Vienna was surrounded by vineyards, and Duke Rudolf IV taxed tavern wine from 1359.
regions.terroir: Limestone and loess on the Nussberg and Kahlenberg, flysch sandstone, gravel and loess on the Bisamberg, and warm Pannonian influence.
regions.grapes: Grüner Veltliner, Riesling, Weißburgunder, Chardonnay, Gemischter Satz field blends (often with Neuburger, Traminer, Welschriesling), Zweigelt, Pinot Noir.
regions.styles: Gemischter Satz field blends, dry whites, some reds, Sekt.
regions.classification: Wiener Gemischter Satz DAC (2013): at least three white varieties planted together, the largest no more than 50 percent and the third at least 10 percent; a Ried name may be given. Other wines are labelled Wien.

regions.name: Bergland
regions.tagline: Small, ambitious vineyards in the Alpine provinces.
regions.summary: Bergland groups the five western and southern provinces of Kärnten (Carinthia), Oberösterreich (Upper Austria), Salzburg, Tirol and Vorarlberg, with about 243 hectares of vines in all. Each is a separate PDO. Carinthia, with vineyards on sunny slopes around the Wörthersee and in the Lavant valley, has grown fastest since its wine law was relaxed in the 2000s; Upper Austria has small vineyards along the Danube near Linz; Tirol and Vorarlberg grow a few hectares in sheltered valleys.
regions.history: Monasteries such as St. Paul im Lavanttal made wine in Carinthia in the Middle Ages, but the Little Ice Age and competition from the east pushed viticulture back. Modern revival began after 1970.
regions.terroir: Varied Alpine soils on sunny, sheltered slopes, often near lakes; cool nights and high frost risk.
regions.grapes: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Blanc, Pinot Noir, Zweigelt, fungus-resistant varieties (Solaris, Muscaris).
regions.styles: Mostly dry whites and some sparkling wine.
regions.classification: Five PDOs: Kärnten, Oberösterreich, Salzburg, Tirol, Vorarlberg.

sources.title: Candiago et al. (2022), geospatial inventory of EU wine PDOs

at-burgenland.name: Burgenland
at-burgenland.summary: The federal-state PDO for Burgenland, used for quality wine from any of its areas that falls outside the DAC rules, for example Cabernet blends, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and most sweet wines from beyond Rust and the Seewinkel DAC rules.
at-burgenland.nerd_note: Many of Burgenland's most famous red blends, such as Gernot Heinrich's Pannobile, appear under the Burgenland origin rather than a DAC.

at-carnuntum.name: Carnuntum
at-carnuntum.grapes: Zweigelt, Blaufränkisch; Grüner Veltliner, Chardonnay, Weißburgunder
at-carnuntum.summary: Carnuntum lies east of Vienna between the Danube and the Leitha hills, named after the Roman legionary town and provincial capital whose ruins dominate Petronell. Its 800-odd hectares of loess, gravel and limestone at Göttlesbrunn, Höflein, Prellenkirchen and on the Spitzerberg are warm and windy, ideal for red wine. Zweigelt is the signature (sold by a growers' group as 'Rubin Carnuntum'), and Blaufränkisch from the Spitzerberg's limestone is the region's most serious wine. The DAC (2019 vintage) covers Zweigelt, Blaufränkisch, Grüner Veltliner, Chardonnay and Weißburgunder, with cuvées at least two-thirds from these.
at-carnuntum.terroir: Loess and gravel terraces, limestone on the Spitzerberg and Hundsheimer Berg; Pannonian warmth with constant wind.
at-carnuntum.nerd_note: Dorli Muhr (Muhr-van der Niepoort) helped revive the Spitzerberg's half-abandoned limestone terraces for Blaufränkisch.

at-eisenberg.name: Eisenberg
at-eisenberg.grapes: Blaufränkisch; Welschriesling only with a Ried name
at-eisenberg.summary: Eisenberg is the southern Burgenland area around the Eisenberg hill and the villages of Deutsch-Schützen, Höll and Moschendorf, near the Hungarian border, with about 525 hectares. The 'iron mountain' has greenschist and iron-rich loam soils that give Blaufränkisch of rare finesse, with dark cherry, pepper and a mineral, slightly bloody note. Since 2023 the Reserve category has gone and the DAC focuses on Blaufränkisch, with Welschriesling allowed for Riedenwein. South Burgenland is also the home of Uhudler, a rustic wine from American hybrid grapes that has its own protected status.
at-eisenberg.terroir: Greenschist (phyllite), iron-rich loam and clay on the Eisenberg and the Deutsch-Schützen hills; warmer and wetter than northern Burgenland.
at-eisenberg.nerd_note: Uhudler, made from American hybrid grapes, spent decades in legal limbo before Burgenland re-authorised it in the 2010s; it is now a regional cult.

at-kamptal.name: Kamptal
at-kamptal.summary: The Kamptal follows the little Kamp river from the Waldviertel down to the Danube plain, with about 3,570 hectares around Langenlois, Austria's largest wine town, and the villages of Zöbing, Gobelsburg, Kammern, Strass and Schönberg. Its fame rests on the Heiligenstein, a ridge of 270-million-year-old desert sandstone that gives some of Austria's greatest Rieslings, and on loess slopes such as the Lamm, Spiegel and Renner that give deep, spicy Grüner Veltliner. Cool air from the Waldviertel cools the vineyards on summer nights, keeping the wines fresh. The DAC (2008) covers Grüner Veltliner and Riesling, with Ortswein and Riedenwein tiers; the ÖTW classification of Erste Lagen began here and in Kremstal.
at-kamptal.terroir: Permian sandstone and conglomerate with volcanic fragments on the Heiligenstein; gneiss and amphibolite on the Gaisberg; loess on the Lamm, Spiegel and Käferberg.
at-kamptal.nerd_note: Schloss Gobelsburg, run by Michael Moosbrugger, belonged to the Cistercians of Zwettl Abbey, and its 'Tradition' wines recreate nineteenth-century cellar methods.

at-karnten.name: Kärnten
at-karnten.summary: Carinthia's PDO, registered in 2004, covers small vineyards on sunny, often lakeside slopes around the Wörthersee, Millstätter See, the Lavant valley and near St. Paul's abbey. Plantings have grown fast since 2000, mostly Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Blanc, Pinot Noir and fungus-resistant varieties.
at-karnten.terroir: Alpine slopes with cool nights; frost risk.

at-kremstal.name: Kremstal
at-kremstal.summary: Kremstal surrounds the old wine town of Krems at the eastern exit of the Wachau, with about 2,240 hectares. West of the town, around Stein and on the Pfaffenberg, the soils are the same primary rock as the Wachau and the Rieslings are equally fine; east and north of Krems, around Rohrendorf, Gedersdorf and Senftenberg, deep loess terraces give rich, spicy Grüner Veltliner. South of the Danube the vineyards around Furth and Palt lie below the great baroque abbey of Göttweig. The DAC (2007) allows Grüner Veltliner and Riesling, with Ortswein and Riedenwein tiers.
at-kremstal.terroir: Gneiss and mica schist at Stein and Senftenberg, deep loess at Krems, Rohrendorf and Gedersdorf.
at-kremstal.nerd_note: The Kremser Sandgrube, recorded in 1208, is the oldest documented vineyard name in Austria.

at-leithaberg.name: Leithaberg
at-leithaberg.created: DAC red from 2008, white from 2009 (EU reg. 2009)
at-leithaberg.grapes: Blaufränkisch (red); Weißburgunder, Chardonnay, Neuburger, Grüner Veltliner and blends (white)
at-leithaberg.summary: Leithaberg covers the western shore of Lake Neusiedl and the slopes of the Leitha hills (Leithagebirge), with Jois, Winden, Breitenbrunn, Purbach, Donnerskirchen, Schützen, Eisenstadt, Großhöflein and St. Georgen. Its soils of Leitha limestone and mica schist give wines with a cool, chalky structure: Blaufränkisch that is fine-boned rather than heavy, and whites from Pinot Blanc, Chardonnay, Neuburger and Grüner Veltliner that are dry, mineral and lightly oaked at most. The DAC was a growers' initiative, launched for reds in 2008 and whites in 2009, and it explicitly asks for 'minerality' rather than power.
at-leithaberg.terroir: Leitha limestone (fossil-rich coral and shell limestone) and mica schist and gneiss on the slopes of the Leithagebirge; the lake's warmth below.
at-leithaberg.nerd_note: A single ancient vine found in 2000 near St. Georgen, in the Leithaberg area, turned out to be a parent of Grüner Veltliner; it was propagated and is now grown again as 'St. Georgen'.

at-mittelburgenland.name: Mittelburgenland
at-mittelburgenland.summary: Mittelburgenland, which calls itself 'Blaufränkischland', covers about 2,000 hectares around Deutschkreutz, Horitschon, Neckenmarkt and Lutzmannsburg on the Hungarian border. Sheltered from the north by the Ödenburg (Sopron) hills and open to Pannonian warmth, its deep, heavy clay soils give Blaufränkisch of dark fruit, firm tannin and spice. It was Austria's second DAC (2005 vintage) and is limited to Blaufränkisch, with Ortswein, Riedenwein and Reserve categories. Roland Velich's Moric, from very old vines at Lutzmannsburg and Neckenmarkt, showed that Mittelburgenland Blaufränkisch could be ethereal rather than merely powerful.
at-mittelburgenland.terroir: Deep, heavy clay and loam with gravel and sand; warm and sheltered.
at-mittelburgenland.nerd_note: Franz Weninger also farms vines across the border in Hungary's Sopron, the same Blaufränkisch landscape split by the 1921 frontier.

at-neusiedlersee.name: Neusiedlersee
at-neusiedlersee.created: DAC from 2011 vintage (sweet wines added 2020; PDO 1996)
at-neusiedlersee.grapes: Zweigelt (dry DAC); white varieties for sweet DAC
at-neusiedlersee.summary: Neusiedlersee covers the north and east shores of Lake Neusiedl, from Gols and Mönchhof to Podersdorf, Illmitz and Apetlon in the Seewinkel, about 6,000 hectares. The shallow steppe lake (315 square kilometres but under 2 metres deep), the salty Seewinkel ponds and the Pannonian heat create two great wine styles. In summer and early autumn, warm days produce juicy Zweigelt and powerful red blends around Gols, where the Pannobile growers (Heinrich, Nittnaus, Achs, Beck, Pittnauer, Preisinger, Renner) set the tone. Then autumn mists off the lake bring noble rot, and Illmitz and Apetlon make Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese of world class; the late Alois Kracher made them famous in the 1990s with his numbered 'Zwischen den Seen' and 'Nouvelle Vague' TBAs. The DAC (2011) is for Zweigelt, classic or Reserve; since 2020 sweet wines from white grapes also qualify.
at-neusiedlersee.terroir: Sand, gravel, loam and black earth (Tschernosem); salty soils in the Seewinkel; the lake moderates frost and feeds autumn mist.
at-neusiedlersee.nerd_note: Gerhard Nekowitsch in Illmitz pioneered Schilfwein, sweet wine from grapes dried on mats woven from the lake's reeds.

at-niederosterreich.name: Niederösterreich
at-niederosterreich.summary: The federal-state PDO for Lower Austria, used for quality wines from anywhere in its eight DAC areas that do not meet (or do not seek) DAC rules: a Kamptal Zweigelt or a Wachau Chardonnay, for example, is labelled Niederösterreich. With 26,732 hectares, it is by far Austria's largest origin.
at-niederosterreich.nerd_note: Austrian Sekt g.U. (with Klassik, Reserve and Große Reserve tiers since 2015) is often labelled with the Niederösterreich origin.

at-oberosterreich.name: Oberösterreich
at-oberosterreich.summary: Upper Austria's PDO (2004) covers a handful of vineyards along the Danube and in the Alpine foreland, with fresh whites and some sparkling wine.
at-oberosterreich.terroir: Alpine slopes with cool nights; frost risk.

at-rosalia.name: Rosalia
at-rosalia.grapes: Blaufränkisch, Zweigelt (red); rosé from one or more red varieties
at-rosalia.summary: Rosalia, Austria's smallest DAC at about 230 hectares, lies on the eastern slopes of the Rosalia hills in the Mattersburg district of northern Burgenland, between the Leithaberg and Mittelburgenland. Its cool, forested hills give Blaufränkisch and Zweigelt with freshness and spice. Rosalia is the only DAC with a protected rosé category, which recognises the area's long tradition of pink wines.
at-rosalia.terroir: Gravel, sand, loam and crystalline rock on the slopes of the Rosaliengebirge, cooler than the lake shore.
at-rosalia.nerd_note: The region takes its name from a chapel to St. Rosalia on the hilltop.

at-ruster-ausbruch.name: Ruster Ausbruch
at-ruster-ausbruch.grapes: One or more white varieties: Furmint, Welschriesling, Weißburgunder, Chardonnay, Gelber Muskateller and others
at-ruster-ausbruch.summary: Ruster Ausbruch is one of the world's great historic sweet wines, made only in the town of Rust on the western shore of Lake Neusiedl. Botrytised berries are picked by hand, berry by berry, and must reach at least 30 degrees KMW, the same as a Trockenbeerenauslese, but the traditional method of soaking or pressing the shrivelled berries in fresh must gives a wine with more acid lift and less cloying sweetness. In the seventeenth century Ausbruch was famous across Europe, and Rust is said to have paid part of the price of its freedom as a royal town in 1681 in barrels of it. A DAC since 2020, it is a tiny production carried by a handful of families who still keep storks nesting on their chimneys.
at-ruster-ausbruch.terroir: Rust's slopes of Leitha limestone and schist face the lake, whose mists bring noble rot in autumn.
at-ruster-ausbruch.nerd_note: Michael Wenzel and Heidi Schröck helped revive Furmint in Rust, the grape of Tokaji, which had almost disappeared from Austria.

at-salzburg.name: Salzburg
at-salzburg.summary: The PDO for the province of Salzburg, registered in 2004, has only a few hectares, notably near Salzburg city; it exists mainly so that growers can sell quality wine with a local origin.
at-salzburg.terroir: Alpine slopes with cool nights; frost risk.

at-steiermark.name: Steiermark
at-steiermark.summary: The federal-state PDO for Styria, covering quality wines that fall outside the three Styrian DACs, including reds such as Zweigelt and Blauburger and many sparkling wines.
at-steiermark.nerd_note: Styria is known for the Klapotetz, a wooden wind-rattle that scares birds from the ripening grapes.

at-sud-oststeiermark.name: Vulkanland Steiermark
at-sud-oststeiermark.grapes: Welschriesling, Weißburgunder, Morillon, Grauburgunder, Riesling, Gelber Muskateller, Sauvignon Blanc, Traminer
at-sud-oststeiermark.summary: The Vulkanland in south-eastern Styria is a hilly landscape of extinct volcanoes, with castles on basalt plugs at Riegersburg and Kapfenstein, about 1,650 hectares of vines and a scattered pattern of small vineyards among orchards and fields. Volcanic basalt and tuff, mixed with sand and loam, give whites of spice and warmth; the Traminer of Klöch is the area's most famous speciality, intensely perfumed with rose petals. Neumeister in Straden and Winkler-Hermaden at Kapfenstein are the leading names. The DAC (2018 vintage) has three tiers; the region was called Süd-Oststeiermark until the change to Vulkanland.
at-sud-oststeiermark.terroir: Basalt, volcanic tuff and ash over sand and clay; warmer and drier than Südsteiermark, with Pannonian influence.
at-sud-oststeiermark.nerd_note: Klöch's Weinbaumuseum and Traminer route celebrate a grape planted on the volcano's slopes for centuries.

at-sudsteiermark.name: Südsteiermark
at-sudsteiermark.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Morillon, Gelber Muskateller, Weißburgunder, Grauburgunder, Welschriesling, Riesling, Traminer
at-sudsteiermark.summary: Südsteiermark is a landscape of steep, green hills along the Slovenian border south of Graz, with about 2,800 hectares around Gamlitz, Ehrenhausen, Leutschach, Spielfeld and the Sausal hills at Kitzeck. Vines grow on gradients of up to about 70 percent, among the steepest in Austria, and the Südsteirische Weinstraße winds along ridges where the vineyards of Austria and Slovenia touch. The wines are dry and aromatic: Sauvignon Blanc with gooseberry, elderflower and cassis-leaf intensity, the piercing grapey Gelber Muskateller, and Morillon (the local name for Chardonnay) that can be as complex as Burgundy from the best Rieden. The DAC (2018 vintage) has Gebietswein, Ortswein and Riedenwein tiers and requires hand harvesting.
at-sudsteiermark.terroir: Opok (marl and calcareous sandstone), sand, gravel and coral limestone in the south; slate and schist in the Sausal, where Kitzeck's vineyards reach over 600 metres. Rainfall is higher than elsewhere in Austria, offset by steep drainage and warm days.
at-sudsteiermark.nerd_note: Tement's Zieregg vineyard straddles the border; the family's Slovenian holdings are bottled as Ciringa.

at-thermenregion.name: Thermenregion
at-thermenregion.grapes: Zierfandler, Rotgipfler, Weißburgunder, Chardonnay, Sankt Laurent, Pinot Noir
at-thermenregion.summary: The Thermenregion runs south from Vienna along the edge of the Vienna Woods to Bad Vöslau, a landscape of spa towns (Baden bei Wien's hot springs give the name) and old monastery estates. Around Gumpoldskirchen, Pfaffstätten and Traiskirchen it grows two rare white grapes found almost nowhere else: Zierfandler (Spätrot) and Rotgipfler, which give rich, spicy, long-lived whites, dry or sweet. Further south, around Tattendorf, Sooß and Bad Vöslau, the hot gravel plain gives fine Sankt Laurent and Pinot Noir. The Thermenregion became Austria's eighteenth and last DAC with the 2023 vintage, with Gebietswein, Ortswein and Riedenwein tiers.
at-thermenregion.terroir: Limestone and calcareous gravel at the foot of the Vienna Woods, warm Pannonian climate, plus the hot, stony Steinfeld plain to the south.
at-thermenregion.nerd_note: Freigut Thallern has belonged to the Cistercian abbey of Heiligenkreuz since 1141, one of the oldest continuously run wine estates in Austria.

at-tirol.name: Tirol
at-tirol.summary: Tyrol's PDO (1999) covers small, sheltered vineyards in the Inn valley and its side valleys, including some of the highest in Austria.
at-tirol.terroir: Alpine slopes with cool nights; frost risk.

at-traisental.name: Traisental
at-traisental.summary: The Traisental, south of the Danube around Traismauer, Herzogenburg and Nußdorf ob der Traisen, is the smallest of Lower Austria's Danube regions. Its vines grow on chalky conglomerate and gravel terraces that give Grüner Veltliner and Riesling with unusual tension and a firm, almost salty finish. The DAC dates from 2006.
at-traisental.terroir: Calcareous conglomerate, gravel and loess on narrow terraces; cool air from the Alpine foothills to the south.
at-traisental.nerd_note: Unlike the crystalline Wachau and Kamptal, the Traisental's best sites are on limestone-rich conglomerate, a reason its Grüner often tastes leaner and more mineral.

at-vorarlberg.name: Vorarlberg
at-vorarlberg.summary: The westernmost PDO (1999), with a few hectares near Lake Constance and in the Rhine valley, close to Swiss and German neighbours.
at-vorarlberg.terroir: Alpine slopes with cool nights; frost risk.

at-wachau.name: Wachau
at-wachau.grapes: Grüner Veltliner, Riesling (Riedenwein only these two); 17 varieties for Gebietswein
at-wachau.summary:
The Wachau is a 36-kilometre stretch of the Danube between Melk and Krems where the river cuts through granite and gneiss hills, and its terraced vineyards, castles and baroque abbeys make it one of the loveliest wine landscapes in Europe (UNESCO World Heritage, 2000). Only about 1,285 hectares of vines grow here, mostly on narrow terraces held up by dry-stone walls, but they produce some of the world's finest dry Grüner Veltliner and Riesling.

The wines are dry and unchaptalised, and since 1983 the growers' association Vinea Wachau has graded them by ripeness: Steinfeder (light, up to 11.5 percent alcohol, named after a feathery grass on the terraces), Federspiel (11.5 to 12.5 percent, named after a falconry lure) and Smaragd (above 12.5 percent, named after the emerald lizards that bask on the walls). A Smaragd Riesling from the Achleiten or Kellerberg combines ripe stone fruit with a cool, stony core and can age for decades. Since the 2020 vintage the Wachau has been a DAC with three tiers: Gebietswein (17 varieties), Ortswein (nine varieties) and Riedenwein, reserved for Grüner Veltliner and Riesling from 157 named Rieden and always hand-picked.

The pioneers include Josef Jamek, who made dry Wachau wines famous in the 1950s and 1960s, and the generation of F.X. Pichler, Franz Hirtzberger, Emmerich Knoll and Franz Prager that followed. The Domäne Wachau cooperative in Dürnstein farms about a third of the area.
at-wachau.terroir: Primary rock (gneiss, amphibolite, mica schist and granulite) on the terraces, loess and sand at the foot of the slopes. The Danube moderates temperatures, warm Pannonian air drifts up the valley from the east and cold air drains from the Waldviertel at night; the Spitzer Graben side valley is notably cooler. Irrigation is often needed on the thin terrace soils.
at-wachau.nerd_note: The Smaragd category is named after the emerald lizard that suns itself on the terrace walls; Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd are trademarks of Vinea Wachau, not legal categories, so only members may use them.

at-wagram.name: Wagram
at-wagram.created: DAC from 2021 vintage (PDO 1996 as Donauland; renamed 2007)
at-wagram.grapes: Grüner Veltliner, Roter Veltliner, Riesling, Pinot Blanc, Pinot Noir and others by tier
at-wagram.summary: The Wagram is a long loess escarpment rising up to 40 metres above the Danube plain north of the river, between Krems and Vienna, together with the Klosterneuburg area south of the river. Its roughly 2,400 hectares are built on loess many metres deep, which gives Grüner Veltliner of creamy weight and spice. The region is also the home of Roter Veltliner, an old and difficult variety (unrelated to Grüner) that here gives rich, nutty whites. Bernhard Ott's biodynamic Grüner from Feuersbrunn made the Wagram's name. The area was called Donauland until 2007 and became a DAC from the 2021 vintage, with Gebietswein, Ortswein and Riedenwein tiers.
at-wagram.terroir: Deep loess over gravel and marine sediments on a south-facing escarpment above the Danube.
at-wagram.nerd_note: The name Wagram comes from 'Wogenrain', the bank of the waves, referring to the ancient shoreline of the Danube.

at-weinviertel.name: Weinviertel
at-weinviertel.grapes: Grüner Veltliner (DAC); many others under Niederösterreich
at-weinviertel.summary:
The Weinviertel, the 'wine quarter' between the Danube, the Manhartsberg and the Czech and Slovak borders, is Austria's largest wine area with about 13,700 hectares, a third of the national vineyard, and in 2025 it produced 989,300 hectolitres. Rolling loess hills, sunflower fields and villages with cellar lanes (Kellergassen) define it. The Weinviertel became Austria's first DAC with the 2002 vintage and limited it to Grüner Veltliner in a fresh, fruity, peppery style (the famous 'Pfefferl'), with Reserve (from 2009) and Große Reserve (since 2020) for richer wines.

The region is diverse: Poysdorf in the north-east is Austria's Sekt base, Falkenstein has limestone cliffs and old castles, Röschitz near the Manhartsberg has granite, and the far north-east near the March river is warm enough for reds.
at-weinviertel.terroir: Loess dominates, with limestone at Falkenstein and the Waschberg, granite near the Manhartsberg; a dry, Pannonian-continental climate.
at-weinviertel.nerd_note: The Weinviertel was Austria's first DAC: its growers chose Grüner Veltliner as the region's sole flagship and launched the appellation with the 2002 vintage.

at-weststeiermark.name: Weststeiermark
at-weststeiermark.grapes: Blauer Wildbacher (Schilcher); white varieties at Ort and Ried level
at-weststeiermark.summary: West Styria, south-west of Graz around Stainz, Deutschlandsberg, Ligist and Wies, is the land of Schilcher, a pale onion-skin to salmon rosé from the Blauer Wildbacher grape. Schilcher has piercing acidity and notes of redcurrant and rhubarb, a love-it-or-hate-it wine drunk locally with cold cuts in the Buschenschanken along the Schilcherweinstraße; modern producers also make it as sparkling wine and as a more structured Ried wine. About 650 hectares grow on gneiss and schist at up to 600 metres. The DAC (2018 vintage) requires hand harvest and covers Schilcher and selected white varieties.
at-weststeiermark.terroir: Gneiss and schist, often steep, at the edge of the Koralpe; cooler and wetter than the rest of Styria.
at-weststeiermark.nerd_note: Blauer Wildbacher may only be labelled Schilcher if it comes from Styria; the word is protected.

at-wien.name: Wien
at-wien.grapes: Grüner Veltliner, Riesling, Weißburgunder, Chardonnay, Gemischter Satz varieties, Zweigelt, Pinot Noir
at-wien.summary: Vienna's own PDO covers about 588 hectares within the city limits, on the Nussberg, Kahlenberg, Bisamberg and Maurer Berg. The wines, mostly white, are drunk largely in the city's Heurigen. Varietal wines and reds are labelled Wien, while field blends that meet the rules become Wiener Gemischter Satz DAC.
at-wien.terroir: Limestone, loess, gravel and flysch on the hills around the city; Pannonian warmth.
at-wien.nerd_note: Vienna claims to be the only capital in the world with significant vineyards inside its borders.

at-wiener-gemischter-satz.name: Wiener Gemischter Satz
at-wiener-gemischter-satz.grapes: At least three white varieties from one vineyard, planted together
at-wiener-gemischter-satz.summary: Gemischter Satz means a 'mixed planting': vineyards where different varieties grow side by side and are picked and fermented together, as was normal before single-variety planting took over. Vienna kept the tradition alive, and Fritz Wieninger and a group of growers turned it into a quality wine and Austria's tenth DAC in 2013. At least three white varieties must be planted together in a Viennese vineyard; the largest may not exceed 50 percent and the third largest must reach at least 10 percent. The wines range from light Heuriger whites to complex single-vineyard blends from the Nussberg or Bisamberg.
at-wiener-gemischter-satz.terroir: Vineyards on the Nussberg (limestone), Bisamberg (loess, gravel) and other Viennese hills.
at-wiener-gemischter-satz.nerd_note: Some Nussberg field blends include up to twenty varieties, among them old Viennese grapes such as Grüner Sylvaner, Rotgipfler and Zierfandler.

sites.name: Ried Achleiten
sites.text: A steep slope of terraced gneiss, amphibolite and serpentine above Weißenkirchen, facing south-east over the Danube. Achleiten Riesling and Grüner Veltliner are famous for their smoky, stony intensity; Prager's and Domäne Wachau's bottlings are benchmarks.

sites.name: Ried Klaus
sites.text: A narrow, steep terrace of gneiss next to the Achleiten at Weißenkirchen and Joching, giving taut, saline Riesling. Prager and Josef Jamek make classic examples.

sites.name: Ried Loibenberg
sites.text: The broad, south-facing hillside above Unterloiben and Oberloiben, one of the warmest sites in the Wachau, of gneiss covered in places with loess. It gives opulent Smaragd Riesling and Grüner. Coordinates are on the slope below the Loibenberg summit.

sites.name: Ried Kellerberg
sites.text: Terraces of gneiss between Dürnstein and Oberloiben, cooled by air flowing down a side gully at night. F.X. Pichler's Kellerberg Riesling and Grüner Veltliner Smaragd are among Austria's most celebrated whites.

sites.name: Ried Steinertal
sites.text: A cool, narrow side valley east of the Loibenberg with gneiss and amphibolite, where the temperature drops sharply at night. Alzinger's and F.X. Pichler's Steinertal Rieslings are known for their cut and finesse.

sites.name: Ried Schütt
sites.text: A site at the mouth of a side valley at Unterloiben whose name refers to the scree washed down from the hills; gravelly gneiss gives powerful yet clear Riesling and Grüner Veltliner.

sites.name: Ried Höhereck
sites.text: A high, steep site between Dürnstein and Loiben on gneiss and mica schist, giving finely structured Riesling and Grüner Veltliner. Alzinger's Höhereck is a reference.

sites.name: Ried Singerriedel
sites.text: A steep, terraced amphitheatre of mica schist and gneiss behind Spitz, facing south-east. Franz Hirtzberger's Singerriedel Riesling Smaragd is one of the great Wachau wines, with floral lift from the cooler western end of the valley.

sites.name: Weingut F.X. Pichler
sites.text: The Oberloiben estate of F.X. and now Lucas Pichler, whose Kellerberg, Loibenberg and Steinertal Smaragds set the standard for powerful, concentrated Wachau wines from the 1980s onward.

sites.name: Weingut Emmerich Knoll
sites.text: A family estate in Unterloiben known for its baroque-style label of St. Urban and for long-lived Riesling and Grüner from the Loibenberg, Kellerberg and Schütt.

sites.name: Weingut Leo Alzinger
sites.text: A small Unterloiben estate whose precise, elegant Rieslings from the Steinertal, Loibenberg and Höhereck rank among the Wachau's finest.

sites.name: Weingut Prager
sites.text: Founded by Franz Prager in Weißenkirchen and run by Toni Bodenstein, a geologist and mayor who mapped the Wachau's soils; famed for Achleiten and Klaus Riesling.

sites.name: Weingut Franz Hirtzberger
sites.text: The Spitz estate of Franz Hirtzberger, long-time president of Vinea Wachau, whose Singerriedel and Honivogl wines are icons of the western Wachau.

sites.name: Nikolaihof
sites.text: An estate in Mautern built on Roman foundations, which claims to be one of the oldest wine estates in Austria. Biodynamic since 1971, it holds Riesling for decades in old casks before release as 'Vinothek'.

sites.name: Domäne Wachau
sites.text: The cooperative of some 250 growers at Dürnstein, farming about a third of the Wachau, with a baroque Kellerschlössel (1715) on the grounds.

sites.name: Dürnstein
sites.text: The blue-towered abbey church and the ruined Kuenringer castle where Richard the Lionheart was held captive in 1192 and 1193 make Dürnstein the Wachau's emblem.

sites.name: Stift Göttweig
sites.text: A baroque Benedictine abbey on a hill south of the Danube opposite Krems, whose vineyards around Furth are now farmed by the Stift Göttweig wine estate.

sites.name: Ried Wachtberg
sites.class: Kremstal Riedenwein site; ÖTW Erste Lage
sites.text: Loess and gneiss terraces rising directly above the old town of Krems, a warm site that gives rich, spicy Grüner Veltliner.

sites.name: Ried Pfaffenberg
sites.class: Kremstal Riedenwein site; ÖTW Erste Lage
sites.text: A steep gneiss site at Stein on the Wachau border, first documented in 1230. Salomon Undhof's and Stift Göttweig's Pfaffenberg Rieslings are classics.

sites.name: Zöbinger Heiligenstein
sites.class: Kamptal Riedenwein site; ÖTW Erste Lage
sites.text: A ridge of Permian desert sandstone and conglomerate, about 270 million years old, rising south of Zöbing. Its name ('holy stone') replaced the earlier 'Hellenstein' (hell's stone), a nod to the heat on its south face. Heiligenstein Riesling from Bründlmayer, Hirsch, Jurtschitsch or Schloss Gobelsburg is among the greatest in Austria.

sites.name: Ried Gaisberg
sites.class: Kamptal Riedenwein site; ÖTW Erste Lage
sites.text: The eastern neighbour of the Heiligenstein above Zöbing and Strass, on crystalline gneiss and amphibolite rather than sandstone, giving finer-boned, more floral Riesling.

sites.name: Ried Lamm
sites.class: Kamptal Riedenwein site; ÖTW Erste Lage
sites.text: A sheltered hollow of deep loess and calcareous soils at the foot of the Heiligenstein in Kammern, a heat trap that gives Austria's most opulent Grüner Veltliners. Bründlmayer's and Hirsch's Lamm are benchmarks.

sites.name: Ried Spiegel
sites.class: Kamptal Riedenwein site; ÖTW Erste Lage
sites.text: A loess slope at Gobelsburg and Langenlois with a cooling breeze, giving elegant, spicy Grüner Veltliner.

sites.name: Weingut Bründlmayer
sites.text: Willi Bründlmayer's Langenlois estate helped define modern Austrian wine, from Heiligenstein Riesling and Lamm Grüner to a celebrated traditional-method Sekt.

sites.name: Schloss Gobelsburg
sites.text: A baroque castle that the Cistercians of Zwettl Abbey owned for centuries; since 1996 run by Michael Moosbrugger with vineyards in Heiligenstein, Gaisberg, Lamm and Grub.

sites.name: Weingut Hiedler
sites.text: Ludwig Hiedler's Langenlois estate, known for slow-fermented, age-worthy Grüner Veltliner and Riesling from Heiligenstein, Gaisberg and Thal.

sites.name: Loisium Langenlois
sites.text: A visitor centre by Steven Holl over a medieval cellar labyrinth beneath Langenlois, telling the story of Kamptal wine.

sites.name: Stift Klosterneuburg
sites.class: Augustinian abbey (1114) and Austria's largest private wine estate
sites.text: The abbey founded by Margrave Leopold III, who became Austria's patron saint, has made wine for about 900 years. Its estate farms vineyards in Vienna, Klosterneuburg, Gumpoldskirchen and Tattendorf, and the nearby school (1860) created the KMW must scale and Zweigelt.

sites.name: Kellergasse Hadres
sites.text: A long lane of small press houses and cellars dug into loess at the edge of Hadres, among the longest Kellergassen in Austria and a classic image of the Weinviertel.

sites.name: Carnuntum Roman city
sites.text: The Roman legionary fortress and provincial capital of Pannonia Superior, where emperors stayed and where the Danube frontier wine trade flowed. The archaeological park at Petronell gives the wine region its name.

sites.name: Freigut Thallern
sites.text: A wine estate at Gumpoldskirchen owned by the abbey of Heiligenkreuz since 1141, known for Zierfandler and Rotgipfler.

sites.name: Rust
sites.text: A small baroque town on Lake Neusiedl with storks on its chimneys, whose sweet Ausbruch made it rich; it paid for its status as a royal free town in 1681 partly with wine.

sites.name: Weingut Feiler-Artinger
sites.text: A family estate in a baroque house in Rust, famous for Ruster Ausbruch and Blaufränkisch-based red blends.

sites.name: Kracher
sites.text: The Illmitz estate of Alois 'Luis' Kracher (died 2007), whose numbered TBAs made Seewinkel botrytis wines world famous; now run by his son Gerhard. Coordinates mark Illmitz.

sites.name: Weingut Gernot und Heike Heinrich
sites.text: A Gols estate that co-founded the Pannobile group of local red blends and moved to biodynamics, with vineyards on the lake's north shore and the Leithaberg.

sites.name: Seewinkel
sites.text: The flat 'lake corner' east of Lake Neusiedl with Illmitz, Apetlon and Podersdorf, dotted with salty ponds; its autumn mists make it one of the world's most reliable sources of noble rot. Part of the Fertő/Neusiedlersee UNESCO landscape (2001) and a national park.

sites.name: Neusiedler See
sites.text: Central Europe's largest steppe lake, 315 square kilometres but at most 1.8 metres deep, shared with Hungary. It warms the region, moderates frost and feeds the autumn mists that bring botrytis.

sites.name: Weingut Prieler
sites.text: The Schützen am Gebirge estate of the Prieler family, whose Goldberg Blaufränkisch from mica schist is a Leithaberg icon.

sites.name: Leithagebirge
sites.text: A low range of Leitha limestone and schist between the Vienna basin and Lake Neusiedl that gives the Leithaberg DAC its mineral character.

sites.name: Rosaliengebirge
sites.text: The forested hills of the Rosalia DAC, crowned by a chapel to St. Rosalia.

sites.name: Weingut Gesellmann
sites.text: A Deutschkreutz estate whose Blaufränkisch from old vines and Opus Eximium blend are Mittelburgenland classics.

sites.name: Moric (Lutzmannsburg)
sites.text: Roland Velich's Moric made its name from century-old Blaufränkisch vines at Lutzmannsburg and Neckenmarkt, fermented and aged without makeup to show soil rather than oak. Coordinates mark Lutzmannsburg village.

sites.name: Eisenberg
sites.text: A greenschist hill near Deutsch-Schützen in southern Burgenland, giving its name to the DAC and to Blaufränkisch of finesse.

sites.name: Ried Zieregg
sites.class: Südsteiermark Riedenwein site; STK Große Lage
sites.text: A steep amphitheatre of coral limestone and marl on the Slovenian border at Ehrenhausen, Tement's flagship. Zieregg Sauvignon Blanc is one of the most complex in the world.

sites.name: Weingut Tement
sites.text: Manfred Tement and his sons Armin and Stefan built the Ehrenhausen estate into Styria's most famous; they also farm across the border as Ciringa.

sites.name: Ried Grassnitzberg
sites.class: Südsteiermark Riedenwein site; STK Große Lage
sites.text: A south-facing slope of opok marl near Spielfeld, giving taut, smoky Sauvignon Blanc. Polz and Tement are key owners.

sites.name: Weingut Polz
sites.text: The Spielfeld estate of Erich and Walter Polz, specialists in Sauvignon Blanc from Grassnitzberg and Hochgrassnitzberg.

sites.name: Weingut Gross
sites.text: A Ratsch family estate known for Sauvignon and Morillon from the Nussberg and for finely tuned, long-lived whites.

sites.name: Weingut Sattlerhof
sites.text: Gamlitz estate of the Sattler family, now organic, known for Sauvignon from the Kranachberg and Pfarrweingarten.

sites.name: Kitzeck im Sausal
sites.text: A hilltop village in the Sausal whose slate vineyards climb to over 600 metres, among the highest in Europe; it has a wine museum and Wohlmuth's estate.

sites.name: Weingut Neumeister
sites.text: The Straden estate of Christoph Neumeister, the Vulkanland's leading producer of Sauvignon Blanc and Weißburgunder on volcanic soils.

sites.name: Weinbaumuseum Klöch
sites.text: The wine museum of Klöch on the slopes of an extinct volcano, the home of Styrian Traminer.

sites.name: Schilcherweinstraße (Stainz)
sites.text: The Schilcher wine route through West Styria starts in Stainz, a market town with a castle, and links Buschenschanken serving the region's pink Blauer Wildbacher wine.

sites.name: Nussberg
sites.text: A limestone hill above Nussdorf and Grinzing with views over the Danube and the city, home of Vienna's finest Gemischter Satz and Riesling and a ring of Heurigen.

sites.name: Bisamberg
sites.class: Vineyard hill north of the Danube
sites.text: Vienna's vineyard hill on the left bank of the Danube above Stammersdorf and Strebersdorf, with loess and gravel soils and a long Heurigen tradition.

sites.name: Weingut Wieninger
sites.text: Fritz Wieninger's Stammersdorf estate led the revival of Vienna wine and the creation of the Gemischter Satz DAC; it farms the Nussberg and Bisamberg biodynamically.

sites.name: Mayer am Pfarrplatz
sites.text: A Heuriger and wine estate in Heiligenstadt in the house where Beethoven lived in 1817, now owned by the Rotes Haus group and known for Nussberg Gemischter Satz.
